Running the xcms workflow interactively

Source: vignettes/xcms-interactive.Rmd
xcms-interactive.Rmd

This vignette walks through the production carpeDIAMS workflow (the gwf module in modules/carpediams/workflow.py) step by step in a single interactive R session. The cluster workflow runs four stages as separate jobs:

[prepare] --> [sample 1..N] --> [filter batch 1..B] --> [finalize] --> MGF

Here the same four stages are plain R calls, and the two fan-out stages are ordinary for loops. Every call goes through carpediams(), so the code you test interactively is the code the cluster runs; only the loop driver differs.

If you just want an MGF from a small dataset, carpediams(input, output) does all of this in one call (stage = "all"). Use the step-by-step version when the dataset is large, when you want to look at the intermediates, or when you are tuning the grouping/filtering settings.

0. Setup: settings in one place 

library(carpeDIAMS)

xcms_path <- "path/to/grouped_xcms.rds"
out_dir   <- "results/carpediams/"
tmp_dir   <- file.path(out_dir, "tmp")
mgf_path  <- file.path(out_dir, "parquets", "all_features.mgf")

# Per-feature spectrum building
grouper   <- pelt_grouper(p0 = 15, Isat = 1e5)
filter_fn <- correlation_filtering(cor_thresh = 0.5, fdr_thresh = 0.01)

n_batches <- 20L

Why do it this way: the grouper and filter are closures, so you configure them once and pass the same objects to every stage. The filter and finalize stages then can’t end up with different settings, which would be easy to cause when copying arguments between calls. Setting tmp_dir explicitly also matters: if you leave it out, carpediams() creates a tempfile() and deletes it when the call returns, so the next stage would find nothing. With an explicit directory, the intermediates survive between calls and you can inspect them, resume from them, or hand them to a cluster job.

1. Load the xcms object 

xobj <- readRDS(xcms_path)

xobj
nrow(xcms::featureDefinitions(xobj))   # must be > 0 (groupChromPeaks() done)
length(xcms::fileNames(xobj))

Why do it this way: carpediams() also accepts the .rds path, but loading the object yourself first lets you check it before any work starts: that features exist, the sample count is what you expect, and the file paths still resolve on this machine. Deserializing a large XcmsExperiment is slow, and it happens only once here. Later stages take the in-memory object, which only tells carpediams() to use the xcms route. They read everything else from tmp_dir and never reload the object.

2. Prepare: subsample, rank, write the manifest 

carpediams(
  input       = xobj,
  output      = mgf_path,
  tmp_dir     = tmp_dir,
  stage       = "prepare",
  subsample   = TRUE,     # apricot picks representative samples
  subset_size = 100L,
  q_prob      = 0.90,
  top_n       = 10L       # top-N most intense samples per feature
)

list.files(tmp_dir)
#> [1] "fd.rds" "manifest.csv" "mssubset.rds" "sample_topfeatures.rds"

manifest <- read.csv(file.path(tmp_dir, "manifest.csv"))
nrow(manifest)

Why do it this way: everything that needs the whole cohort happens here, once: building the feature × sample intensity matrix, the apricot subsampling, and ranking which samples are the top-N for each feature. Each sample then gets a small precomputed list of the features it contributes to, so the per-sample step never rescans the full matrix. manifest.csv is the only thing the next loop needs, and it is a plain CSV, so you can check it in R just as gwf would.

3. Sample stage: one sample at a time 

for (sid in manifest$sample_idx) {
  done <- file.exists(file.path(tmp_dir, sprintf(
    c("sample_%d_pool.parquet", "sample_%d_pointers.parquet"), sid)))
  if (all(done)) next                     # resume: skip finished samples

  carpediams(
    input      = xobj,
    output     = mgf_path,
    tmp_dir    = tmp_dir,
    stage      = "sample",
    sample_idx = sid,
    ppm        = 20,
    rt_buffer  = 5
  )
}

Why do it this way: each iteration reads one mzML, pulls out the MS1 and MS2 scans around that sample’s qualifying features, and writes them to two parquet files. It then returns, so memory goes back down to one sample’s worth. The iterations are fully independent:

  • A crash in sample 137 leaves samples 1–136 on disk. Rerun the loop and the file.exists() check skips straight to where it stopped.
  • Each iteration is exactly one gwf batch_XXXX target. To parallelize, swap the for for furrr::future_walk() (or parallel::mclapply()) without touching the body.
  • Pass the same ppm / rt_buffer to every sample. They shape what gets written, and mixed values give inconsistent pools.

Sanity check before moving on:

expected <- c(sprintf("sample_%d_pool.parquet",     manifest$sample_idx),
              sprintf("sample_%d_pointers.parquet", manifest$sample_idx))
setdiff(expected, list.files(tmp_dir))   # character(0) = all present

4. Filter stage: features in batches 

for (b in seq_len(n_batches)) {
  batch_file <- file.path(tmp_dir, sprintf("features_batch_%d.parquet", b))
  if (file.exists(batch_file)) next       # resume: skip finished batches

  carpediams(
    input     = xobj,
    output    = mgf_path,
    tmp_dir   = tmp_dir,
    stage     = "filter",
    batch_idx = b,
    n_batches = n_batches,
    grouper   = grouper,
    filter_fn = filter_fn
  )
}

Why do it this way: this is the heavy step. For every feature it combines the pooled fragments from all of its top-N samples, groups fragment m/z values with grouper, correlates each group’s elution profile against MS1, and keeps the groups that pass filter_fn. Splitting the features into n_batches contiguous chunks gives you:

  • Bounded memory. Only one batch of features is in memory at a time. On the cluster each batch is a separate 256 GB job; interactively, raise n_batches until a batch fits on your machine.

  • Cheap parameter tuning. Run a single batch (b <- 1) with a candidate grouper / filter_fn, look at the result, and only then run the rest:

    res <- arrow::read_parquet(file.path(tmp_dir, "features_batch_1.parquet"))
length(unique(res$feature_id))

  • Isolated failures. Each batch writes its own features_batch_<b>.parquet, so a failed batch is rerun on its own.

The sample parquets from step 3 are inputs only, so you can redo the filter stage with new settings as often as you like without rerunning the per-sample extraction. Delete the old batch files first (unlink(Sys.glob(file.path(tmp_dir, "features_batch_*.parquet")))). Otherwise the resume check skips them, and finalize combines every features_batch_* file it finds, including leftovers from a run with a different n_batches.

5. Finalize: combine batches and write the MGF 

carpediams(
  input     = xobj,
  output    = mgf_path,
  tmp_dir   = tmp_dir,
  stage     = "finalize",
  grouper   = grouper,
  filter_fn = filter_fn,
  ion_mode  = "POSITIVE"
)
#> ✔ Done: N features -> results/carpediams/parquets/all_features.mgf

Why do it this way: once the batches exist, finalize does no spectral work. It finds every features_batch_*.parquet, row-binds them, and writes one MGF block per feature, so it is fast and cheap to rerun (e.g. to switch ion_mode). Features that ended up without a usable spectrum still get a block, with a DeconvERROR title. Nothing is silently dropped, and the MGF can be reconciled 1:1 against featureDefinitions(xobj). grouper / filter_fn are passed only so that, if no batch files were found, the fallback recomputes everything with the same settings and not the package defaults.

The MGF is the handoff to the annotation module (annotate --input all_features.mgf ...), the same as the last gwf target.

Cleanup

tmp_dir is yours to manage in split-stage mode. Keep it while you iterate on filter settings; delete it once the MGF is validated:

unlink(tmp_dir, recursive = TRUE)

Step here gwf target Script
2. Prepare build_scan_info 00_build_scan_info.R
3. Sample loop batch_XXXX 01_build_samples.R
4. Filter loop clean_XXXX 02_filter_features.R
5. Finalize make_mgf 03_make_mgf.R
